title: Oracle Global Temporary Table: Examples, Indexes and Stats
description: Learn how an Oracle global temporary table works, ON COMMIT DELETE vs PRESERVE ROWS, indexes, ORA-14452, statistics and private temporary tables.

ORA-14452 output was shown only for CREATE INDEX, which is the case the error text describes.

data.text: An Oracle global temporary table (GTT) is a table whose definition is permanent but whose rows are private to each session and disappear automatically. You create it once with CREATE GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE, and then every session can insert into it, see only its own rows, and get an empty table back after a commit or at logout, depending on the ON COMMIT clause.

This tutorial shows both kinds of global temporary table on a small orders table, explains what Oracle does behind the scenes, and covers the parts that trip people up: indexes, DDL errors, optimizer statistics and the newer private temporary tables.
What is a global temporary table in Oracle?

A normal table stores rows that every session can see once they are committed. A global temporary table keeps the table definition in the data dictionary like any other table, but the data belongs to the session that inserted it. Two sessions can use the same GTT at the same time and never see each other's rows.
The word "global" refers to the definition, not the data. The table, its columns, its indexes and its grants are shared by everyone. The rows are not.

Oracle does not allocate any storage when you create the table. A temporary segment is allocated in a temporary tablespace when a session first inserts a row. By default that is the temporary tablespace of the user who created the table. When the transaction or session ends, Oracle releases the segment.
ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS vs ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS
The ON COMMIT clause decides how long the rows live:

content: When the session ends, or when the session runs TRUNCATE

data.text: If you leave out the ON COMMIT clause, you get DELETE ROWS. Many people forget this and are surprised when their data vanishes after the first commit.
Sample setup
Run this in any schema where you can create tables. The orders table is a normal permanent table. We will use global temporary tables to build a per-session report on top of it.

data.caption: Sample orders table

data.text: Example 1: transaction-specific GTT (ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS)
This type is useful for scratch data you need only inside one transaction, for example staging rows before a single INSERT ... SELECT into a permanent table.
Step 1: create the table

data.caption: Transaction-specific global temporary table

data.text: Step 2: insert and query in the same transaction
The four PAID orders are visible because you are still inside the transaction that inserted them.
Step 3: commit and query again

data.code:
COMMIT;

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM gtt_order_stage;

data.text: The commit ended the transaction, so Oracle truncated this session's rows. A ROLLBACK has the same effect. Nothing was deleted from the orders table, only the temporary rows are gone.

Any statement that commits ends the transaction, and DDL statements commit implicitly. If you run a CREATE INDEX or any other DDL in the middle of your work, the rows in an ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS table are gone after it.
Example 2: session-specific GTT (ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS)
This type keeps rows across commits until the session ends. Use it when a session builds intermediate results in several steps, such as a report that runs a few queries and commits in between.
Step 1: create and fill the table

data.caption: Session-specific global temporary table

data.text: The rows survived the commit. They stay until this session logs out or runs TRUNCATE on the table.
Step 2: query from a second session
Open a second connection as the same user (or as another user with SELECT privilege on the table) and run the same query:

data.code: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM gtt_customer_totals;
data.caption: Run in session 2

data.text: Session 2 sees the table but none of session 1's rows. If session 2 inserts its own rows, session 1 will not see them either. Neither session can block the other on this data, because they never touch the same rows.
Step 3: clear the rows without logging out

data.code: TRUNCATE TABLE gtt_customer_totals;

data.text: On a global temporary table, TRUNCATE removes only the current session's rows. Other sessions keep theirs. It also releases the session's binding to the table, which matters for the DDL rules in the next section.
Check whether a table is temporary
The TEMPORARY and DURATION columns of USER_TABLES tell you if a table is a GTT and which ON COMMIT setting it uses:

data.code:
SELECT table_name, temporary, duration
  FROM user_tables
 WHERE table_name LIKE 'GTT%'
 ORDER BY table_name;

TABLE_NAME            T DURATION
--------------------- - ---------------
GTT_CUSTOMER_TOTALS   Y SYS$SESSION
GTT_ORDER_STAGE       Y SYS$TRANSACTION
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: SYS$TRANSACTION means ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS and SYS$SESSION means ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS.
Using a GTT inside PL/SQL
A common pattern is a procedure that fills a GTT and then runs one or more queries against it. The table is created once, during deployment. The procedure only inserts and reads.

data.code:
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE top_customers_report (p_min_total IN NUMBER) AS
BEGIN
  DELETE FROM gtt_customer_totals;  -- clear rows from an earlier call in this session

  INSERT INTO gtt_customer_totals (customer_id, order_count, total_amount)
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*), SUM(amount)
    FROM orders
   WHERE status = 'PAID'
   GROUP BY customer_id;

  FOR r IN (SELECT customer_id, total_amount
              FROM gtt_customer_totals
             WHERE total_amount >= p_min_total
             ORDER BY total_amount DESC)
  LOOP
    DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Customer ' || r.customer_id || ': ' || r.total_amount);
  END LOOP;
END;
/

SET SERVEROUTPUT ON
EXEC top_customers_report(2000)
data.caption: Procedure that uses a session-specific GTT

data.code:
Customer 3: 6200
Customer 1: 2500
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: The DELETE at the start matters. Because the table is ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS, rows from an earlier call in the same session would still be there. A DELETE is used here instead of TRUNCATE because TRUNCATE is DDL and would need EXECUTE IMMEDIATE and an implicit commit.

Connection pools reuse sessions. With ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS, rows left by one request can still be there when the next request gets the same pooled session. Always clear the table at the start of the unit of work, as the procedure above does.
Indexes and DDL on global temporary tables
You can create indexes on a global temporary table. The index is temporary too: its entries have the same session or transaction scope as the table rows.

The catch is when you can run DDL. Oracle allows ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE and CREATE INDEX on a GTT only when no session is bound to it. A session becomes bound with its first INSERT. It is released by TRUNCATE, by ending the session, or, for an ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS table, by COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
Suppose session 1 from Example 2 still has rows in gtt_customer_totals. Another session tries to add an index:

data.code: CREATE INDEX gtt_cust_tot_ix ON gtt_customer_totals (customer_id);
data.caption: Run while session 1 still holds rows

data.code: ORA-14452: attempt to create, alter or drop an index on temporary table already in use
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: The fix is in Oracle's action text for this error: every session using a session-specific GTT must truncate it (or disconnect), and every transaction using a transaction-specific GTT must end. In practice, create indexes during deployment, before the application starts using the table. To find the sessions holding the table, look for sessions with a temporary segment on it in V$TEMPSEG_USAGE, or simply schedule the change in a maintenance window.
Optimizer statistics on global temporary tables

The optimizer needs statistics to pick a good plan, and GTTs are tricky because each session can have very different data. Oracle Database 12c added the table preference GLOBAL_TEMP_TABLE_STATS, which has two values:

items.content: SESSION: statistics gathered with DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS are used only by the session that gathered them, and are deleted when that session ends.
SHARED: all sessions see the same set of statistics, which is how releases before 12c worked.

data.text: During optimization, Oracle first looks for session-specific statistics on the GTT and uses them if they exist. Otherwise it uses shared statistics if any exist. Here is how to check the preference and gather session statistics after loading rows:

data.caption: Gather and inspect GTT statistics

data.code:
PREF
--------
SESSION

TABLE_NAME            NUM_ROWS SCOPE
--------------------- -------- -------
GTT_CUSTOMER_TOTALS          3 SESSION
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: The SCOPE column of USER_TAB_STATISTICS shows whether a row of statistics is session-specific or shared. The first result depends on your database settings, so check it on your system rather than assuming.

Two more details from the Oracle SQL Tuning Guide are worth knowing. For a transaction-specific (DELETE ROWS) GTT, GATHER_TABLE_STATS does not commit, so your rows are not wiped by gathering statistics. For a session-specific (PRESERVE ROWS) GTT, it does commit. Also, CREATE GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE ... AS SELECT gathers statistics automatically.
Global temporary tables vs private temporary tables

Oracle Database 18c added private temporary tables. Both the definition and the data of a private temporary table are visible only to the session that created it, and the definition is stored in memory. Their names must start with the prefix set by PRIVATE_TEMP_TABLE_PREFIX, which is ORA$PTT_ by default.

data.caption: Private temporary table (Oracle 18c and later)

content: Used in views, triggers, stored code

data.text: Choose a global temporary table for application code that runs every day: you define it once, index it, and reference it from packages. A private temporary table suits ad hoc scripts and cases where you cannot or do not want to create a permanent dictionary object.
Common mistakes
Creating the table inside a procedure on every run

Developers coming from SQL Server often create a temp table at the start of a procedure and drop it at the end. In Oracle that means dynamic DDL, implicit commits and ORA-14452 when sessions overlap. Oracle's own guidance is that you create a temporary table for the database itself, not for every stored procedure. Create the GTT once and reuse it.
Forgetting the default is DELETE ROWS

Without an ON COMMIT clause the table is transaction-specific. If your code commits between filling the table and reading it, the table is empty. Pick the clause on purpose and write it out every time.
Expecting other sessions to see the data
A GTT cannot be used to pass data between sessions, jobs or users. Each session has its own rows. Use a permanent table if another session must read the data.
Expecting the data to survive a failure
Backup and recovery are not available for temporary table data. Anything you need to keep must be copied to a permanent table.
Hitting a restriction at deployment time

In Oracle 19c, temporary tables cannot be partitioned, clustered or index-organized, cannot have foreign key constraints, cannot contain nested table columns, cannot have INVISIBLE columns, and do not support parallel UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE or distributed transactions.
Performance tips

items.content: Index the GTT columns you join or filter on, just like a permanent table. Create the indexes at deployment time.
After loading a large number of rows, gather statistics in the session (with the SESSION preference) so the optimizer does not guess the row count.

Consider setting TEMP_UNDO_ENABLED to TRUE (Oracle 12c and later, COMPATIBLE 12.0.0 or higher). It stores undo for temporary objects separately from permanent undo, which Oracle documents as reducing the overall undo and redo the database generates. It must be set before the session first uses a temporary object, because it cannot be changed once that session has temporary objects using undo.
If many small GTT operations waste space in a temporary tablespace with a large extent size, the GTT can be placed in its own temporary tablespace with the TABLESPACE clause.
Do not use a GTT where a single SQL statement (a join, a WITH clause or an analytic function) can do the job. A GTT adds an extra write and read of the data.

data.text: Because GTT data lives in a temporary tablespace, a session that loads a lot of rows uses TEMP space. Size the temporary tablespace with that in mind and monitor it during heavy batch runs.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS and ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS?
DELETE ROWS (the default) empties the session's rows at the end of every transaction. PRESERVE ROWS keeps them across commits until the session ends or truncates the table.
Can multiple sessions use the same global temporary table at the same time?
Yes. That is what the table is built for. Each session sees and changes only its own rows, so sessions do not block each other on the data.
Can we create an index on a global temporary table in Oracle?
Yes. The index is also temporary and has the same scope as the table data. You can only create it when no session is bound to the table, otherwise you get ORA-14452.
Does a global temporary table generate redo?

The table data itself is temporary, but DML on a GTT still generates undo, and with the default settings that undo is protected by redo. Setting TEMP_UNDO_ENABLED to TRUE keeps undo for temporary objects in the temporary tablespace and reduces this redo.
How do I drop a global temporary table that is in use?
All sessions using it must first truncate it or disconnect, and transactions using a DELETE ROWS table must end. Then DROP TABLE works like it does for a normal table.
Summary

items.content: A GTT has a shared definition and session-private rows
ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS (default) clears rows at commit; PRESERVE ROWS clears them at session end
Create the GTT once at deployment, never inside procedures
Clear the table at the start of each unit of work when sessions are pooled
Create indexes before sessions start using the table to avoid ORA-14452
Gather session statistics after big loads; check the SCOPE column
Use private temporary tables (18c+) for ad hoc, session-only work

linkedin.post:
Your Oracle report procedure works in testing but returns an empty result in production. Check your temporary table.

Global temporary tables (GTT) in Oracle have a shared definition but private rows for each session. A few rules that save hours of debugging:

→ The default is ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS. One COMMIT, or any DDL, and your rows are gone.
→ Use ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS when the data must survive commits within a session.
→ Create the GTT once at deployment. Creating it inside a procedure, SQL Server style, leads to implicit commits and ORA-14452.
→ Connection pools reuse sessions, so PRESERVE ROWS data can leak into the next request. Clear the table at the start of each call.
→ Since 12c, statistics on a GTT can be session-specific (GLOBAL_TEMP_TABLE_STATS = SESSION). Gather them after a big load.

Bonus: Oracle 18c added private temporary tables (ORA$PTT_ prefix) for session-only, ad hoc work.

Do you use GTTs in your PL/SQL code, or do you prefer a WITH clause?
